lesson.title: One Key, Two Jobs: The Speed and the Problem of Symmetric Encryption
lesson.summary: Symmetric encryption uses the exact same secret key to both lock and unlock data, which makes it extremely fast, but it leaves open the hard problem of how two parties get that key to each other securely in the first place.
lesson.body:
Symmetric encryption is the most intuitive form of cryptography, in the sense that it works the way a physical lock works. You and I agree on a key beforehand. I use that key to turn your readable message, the plaintext, into scrambled, unreadable ciphertext. You use the exact same key to turn that ciphertext back into the original plaintext. The same key does both jobs, which is where the name comes from. The modern standard for this kind of encryption is AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard, and it is what protects the bulk of encrypted traffic on the internet today, including, as the previous chapter mentioned, the data flowing through an already established SSH session.

Symmetric ciphers are fast, and that speed is not incidental, it is the whole reason they are still used everywhere despite the problem described below. Algorithms like AES are built from relatively simple, repeated operations on fixed size blocks of bits, operations that modern CPUs can execute extremely efficiently, often with dedicated hardware instructions built specifically to accelerate them. That makes symmetric encryption the right tool for encrypting large volumes of data quickly: a video stream, a file transfer, or the ongoing traffic of a remote terminal session.

The catch is what cryptographers call the key distribution problem, and it is worth working through concretely because it is not obvious at first. Suppose Alice wants to send Bob a file, encrypted so that no one else can read it. She and Bob have never met and have no shared secret already. If Alice simply emails Bob the encryption key alongside the encrypted file, or in a separate email, anyone who can read Alice's or Bob's email, including whoever might already be intercepting their traffic, gets both the lock and the key. If Alice calls Bob on the phone and reads the key aloud, that does not scale past two people who happen to have a trusted phone line, and it still fails completely if the phone line itself is already compromised. The fundamental issue is that to send the key securely, Alice would seemingly need an already secure channel, but if she had one of those, she would not need to send a key at all, she could just send the message directly. Symmetric encryption alone cannot break out of that circle.

This is exactly the wall that SSH, described in the previous chapter, has to get past before it can start encrypting a session with a fast symmetric cipher, and it is the same wall that TLS, covered later in this unit, runs into every time a browser connects to a website it has never talked to before. The next chapter introduces the tool that breaks the circle: public key cryptography, which lets two strangers, with no prior shared secret, agree on a key over a channel that someone else might be watching the entire time.
